Mira and Jonah reached the forest aquarium eager to see the river fish exhibit. Their map sent them toward the east hall, but a cleaning barrier blocked that hallway. The map did not show another way. A new blue sign pointed toward the west hall. Mira noticed that the sign stood near the entrance, where visitors could see it before reaching the barrier. Several families were already walking west.

Beside the sign, a river-habitat poster showed fish sheltering beneath smooth stones. The poster reminded Jonah what they hoped to see, but it did not say which hallway was open. They followed the west corridor past a display of water plants. For a moment, Jonah thought they might have gone too far because the river fish were nowhere in sight. Around a bend, Mira spotted a wide tank filled with smooth stones. She waited until something flickered between them. Small fish darted into the open water, then returned to the gaps. They had reached the exhibit without crossing the closed hall.

On the way out, they looked at the map and sign side by side. The map was useful for finding the aquarium, yet it had been printed before the cleaning work. The sign described what visitors could do that day. Mira had also seen people using the west hall, which supported the direction on the sign. She did not assume the east hall would remain closed forever. If they came back another day, they would check the current signs before choosing a route.
options: They checked a newer sign when an older map led to a closed hall.
The visitors noticed that the east hallway was closed for cleaning.
The visitors saw that a new blue sign pointed toward the west hall.
They found the river fish exhibit without entering the closed hall.

item.passage:
Mira and Jonah visited the aquarium’s river fish exhibit before the keeper dimmed its lights for the evening display. Several small fish crossed the open water in front of the glass. As the lights dimmed, the fish slipped behind the rocks. Soon the open part of the display looked almost empty. Jonah wondered if the fish had been moved elsewhere. Mira looked closely along the bottom and could still see a few tails moving in the gaps.

A card beside the display explained that the rocks gave the fish places to shelter, but it did not say that every fish would hide whenever the light changed. The pair watched for several minutes. One fish came out briefly, then turned back when a larger fish passed. Their observation supported a narrower idea: many of the small fish were using the rocks at that moment. It did not prove why every individual fish moved.

Before leaving, Jonah wrote down what they had seen in order. First the lights changed; next the fish moved toward the stones; then the open water looked quiet. Recording that sequence helped him explain why the display seemed empty without claiming that the fish had vanished. He planned to look again during the brighter morning display to see whether their positions changed.
options: The fish crossed open water before the lights changed.
The keeper dimmed the lights for an evening display.
Jonah wondered whether the fish had been moved.
As the lights dimmed, the small fish slipped behind the rocks.

Mira and Jonah set out on the woodland bike trail with a printed route to the lookout. Rain had fallen overnight. At the first fork, deep ruts cut across the lower path shown on their map. A bicycle wheel could slip into one of them. Fresh orange arrows marked a higher path. Mira stopped to check where the arrows led before they moved their bicycles.

The upper path curved through pines and stayed inside the marked riding area. Its soil felt firm beneath their shoes, so they walked their bicycles uphill. Near the top, loose gravel made the slope harder to climb. Mira slowed down and kept both hands on her handlebars. From one bend, they could still see the muddy lower trail below them. They did not need to test the ruts to know that the lower route was a poor choice that morning. Around the final turn, the trees opened and the lookout came into view.

At the lookout, Jonah compared the printed route with the path they had taken. The paper still showed where the lower trail went, but it could not show how rain had changed its surface. The fresh arrows offered a route, and the firm ground gave the pair another reason to use it. They had observed the mud, checked the marked path, and reached the lookout safely. On a drier day, the lower trail might be usable again; the condition of a route can change.
options: They reached the lookout on firm ground.
The visitors saw that fresh orange arrows marked a higher path.
They used fresh route arrows to avoid the muddy lower bike path.
The visitors noticed that rain had left the lower path muddy.

item.passage:
Halfway through their forest ride, Jonah noticed that steering felt heavier than it had at the start. He stopped at a rest bench and pressed the front tire. It bent more than the rear one. Mira listened as he turned the wheel and heard a faint hiss near the valve. They checked the rubber surface first and saw no sharp object. Then Jonah found that the valve had been left loose after the tire was filled that morning.

They tightened the valve, used the pump at the rest stop, and waited. The front tire stayed firm through a slow test ride on level ground. Mira wrote down the order of their checks because a soft tire could have more than one cause. The hiss near the valve was a useful clue, but the tire holding air after the valve was secured gave them stronger evidence for the explanation.

At the next trail sign, they stopped once more. The tire still felt firm. Jonah did not claim that a loose valve always causes a soft tire; a puncture would require a different repair. In this case, however, their observation, the small change they made, and the result supported a reasonable conclusion about what had happened.
options: Jonah stopped at a rest bench along the trail.
They saw no sharp object on the rubber surface.
The front tire bent more than the rear tire.
A faint hiss came from the valve while the front tire felt soft.

At the forest-edge farm, Mira studied two sets of wheel marks crossing the lane near a shed. One set was pale and dry. The other cut through soft soil where the ridges still crumbled at the edges. A tractor stood nearby with damp earth on its tires. Jonah guessed that the fresh marks had been made that morning, but Mira wanted to separate what they could see from what they merely suspected.

The farm notice said machinery had moved supplies after a brief shower. That information fit the damp marks, yet it did not identify which machine had left each track. They could observe the width and depth of the marks, and they could see that the wet soil inside them had not dried like the older tracks. The pair recorded those details before choosing an explanation.

Mira thought a heavy vehicle had probably crossed the lane more recently than the vehicle that made the pale marks. She could not prove the exact time or driver from tracks alone. Jonah added that the tractor’s muddy tires made it a plausible source, but another farm machine might have similar tires. Their field note stated the strongest claim the evidence supported and left the uncertain part open for the farmer to confirm.
options: A tractor stood beside the shed.
Jonah guessed the marks had been made that morning.
The older wheel marks were pale and dry.
The newer wheel marks cut through soft soil and still had loose edges.

Jonah revised his first thought in his notebook. He wrote what changed, what the fish did, and what Mira could still see. The open water had become quiet, yet the moving tails showed that the fish had not vanished. Mira wanted to watch again during a brighter display before making a broader claim about their behaviour. For now, the strongest inference was limited to the fish sheltering behind the stones at that time. A careful observer could point to the movement in the gaps and explain why an apparently empty exhibit was still home to the fish.

The loose valve supplied a possible cause, and the tire holding air after they closed it offered a further check.
